stem: A client with a life-threatening fungal infection is receiving conventional amphotericin B and has a mildly elevated baseline creatinine. Which trend should the nurse prioritize during therapy?

options.A: A gradual bilirubin increase with stable creatinine and electrolytes, because hepatotoxicity is the principal dose-limiting toxicity of conventional amphotericin B.
options.B: A progressive fall in fasting glucose with unchanged renal function, because hypoglycemia is the characteristic early toxicity used to guide amphotericin B dosing.
options.C: A rising serum creatinine with falling potassium or magnesium, because renal dysfunction and electrolyte depletion are important amphotericin B toxicities requiring close review.
options.D: A mild leukocytosis with stable renal function and electrolytes, because white-cell elevation is the primary laboratory trend that determines treatment intolerance.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling for conventional amphotericin B recommends frequent renal-function monitoring and regular serum-electrolyte monitoring, particularly magnesium and potassium. The adverse-reaction section lists decreased renal function, azotemia, hypokalemia, renal tubular acidosis, nephrocalcinosis, elevations in BUN and serum creatinine, and hypomagnesemia. Therefore a rising creatinine together with falling potassium or magnesium is the priority trend. A and D can represent laboratory changes reported during therapy but do not supersede the directly emphasized renal/electrolyte toxicity pattern. B describes a toxicity pattern not identified as the characteristic monitoring concern in the label.
educational_objective: During conventional amphotericin B therapy, monitor renal function frequently and potassium and magnesium regularly, recognizing rising creatinine with electrolyte depletion as a clinically important toxicity pattern.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_document_title: Amphotericin B for Injection USP — Prescribing Information
source_version_date: Current exact DailyMed set; labeling section date January 3, 2022
source_locator: Precautions > General: use with care in reduced renal function and monitor renal function frequently. Precautions > Laboratory Tests: monitor renal function frequently and serum electrolytes, particularly magnesium and potassium, regularly. Adverse Reactions > Renal and Altered Laboratory Findings: decreased renal function, azotemia, hypokalemia, renal tubular acidosis, nephrocalcinosis, acute renal failure, elevations of BUN/serum creatinine, and hypomagnesemia are reported.
source_claim_supported: Conventional amphotericin B can cause renal dysfunction and potassium/magnesium abnormalities; labeling emphasizes frequent renal-function and regular electrolyte monitoring.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed pp. 38–41: evaluate client response to medications, monitor laboratory values and adverse effects, administer high-risk medications safely, and intervene when medication-related toxicity develops.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — conventional amphotericin B nephrotoxicity and electrolyte monitoring
correction_summary: Rebuilt all options to remove absolute-word cueing and use comparable laboratory-trend alternatives while preserving the source-supported renal and electrolyte monitoring construct.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Antifungal therapy — conventional amphotericin B nephrotoxicity and electrolyte depletion
audit_findings.stem: PASS — clearly specifies conventional amphotericin B and a client with preexisting renal vulnerability, creating a focused toxicity-monitoring task.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — liver tests are monitored and abnormalities can occur, but stable renal/electrolyte status makes this less characteristic of the major dose-limiting toxicity emphasized in the label.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — glucose monitoring can be clinically relevant in many settings, but progressive hypoglycemia is not the characteristic amphotericin B toxicity pattern described in the prescribing information.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS — directly matches the label's frequent renal monitoring and potassium/magnesium toxicity profile; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — leukocytosis can be reported but does not replace renal and electrolyte surveillance as the priority treatment-toxicity trend.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — C is the only option that combines two laboratory domains specifically emphasized for ongoing toxicity surveillance.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A and D may reflect nonspecific or reported changes but lack the directly prioritized nephrotoxicity/electrolyte pattern; B is not the characteristic toxicity.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — options are similar in length, laboratory structure, and clinical specificity, with no keyed-only absolute wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly includes laboratory and adverse-effect monitoring during medication therapy.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether hepatic or hematologic changes could be equally important; the label specifically directs frequent renal-function monitoring and regular potassium/magnesium monitoring and lists renal dysfunction as a major adverse-reaction domain, leaving C uniquely best.
